chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Maḥbūb, from Abī Ayyūb, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:

Whoever brandishes a weapon in a city from among the cities and wounds, retaliation shall be taken from him and he shall be exiled from that town. And whoever brandishes a weapon outside the cities, strikes and wounds, and takes wealth but does not kill, then he is a muḥārib, so his recompense is the recompense of the muḥārib; and his case is up to the Imam: if he wishes, he kills him; if he wishes, he crucifies him; and if he wishes, he cuts off his hand and foot.

He said: And if he strikes, kills, and takes wealth, then it is upon the Imam to cut off his right hand for the theft, then hand him over to the heirs of the slain, so they may pursue him for the wealth, then kill him.

He said: Then Abū ʿUbaydah said to him, “May Allah set you aright, what do you think if the heirs of the slain pardon him?” He said: So Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: “If they pardon him, then it is still upon the Imam to kill him, because he has indeed warred against Allah, killed, and stolen.”

He said: Then Abū ʿUbaydah said to him, “What do you think if the heirs of the slain want to take blood-money from him and leave him, do they have that right?” He said: So he said: “No. Killing is upon him.”

key_terms.أَوْلِيَاءِ الْمَقْتُولِ: the heirs or legal claimants of the slain person
key_terms.الدِّيَةَ: blood-money paid in compensation for killing
key_terms.الْإِمَامِ: the legitimate authority who implements the legal ruling
key_terms.الْقَتْلُ: execution or killing as the imposed punishment
key_terms.مُحَارِبٌ: one who wages violent hostility and armed aggression
key_terms.يَقْطَعَ يَدَهُ الْيُمْنَى: cuts off his right hand as punishment for theft

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling in Shiʿi hadith on a muḥārib who attacks people, steals wealth, and kills?
ai.summary: This hadith sets out legal rulings concerning one who openly bears arms, wounds people, seizes wealth, and in some cases kills, distinguishing between cases and their punishments. It emphasizes the Imam’s authority in applying the penalties of muḥārabah and clarifies that in cases combining violent aggression, killing, and theft, the prescribed punishment remains binding even if the slain person’s heirs wish to pardon or accept blood-money.
